A.explanation: Both $mgv$ and $Mgv\sin\theta$ equal the rate of work done on P, so 1 and 2 are correct.

B.explanation: Statement 1 is correct but statement 2 also gives the same rate of gain of gravitational potential energy by P.

C.explanation: Statement 2 is correct but statement 3 adds the two rates and does not represent energy per unit time to P alone.

D.explanation: Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 is also correct because the tension power from descending Q equals the power to P.

hints: Notice P moves up the slope at constant velocity $v$ while Q moves vertically down, so energy transferred per unit time means power $P = Fv$.
Connect the string tension to the hanging mass: with no acceleration and no friction, tension equals weight $mg$ of Q and also balances $Mg\sin\theta$ for P.
Compare the vertical speed of P, which is $v\sin\theta$ up the $\theta$ slope, with the vertical speed $v$ of Q to see why $mgv$ must equal $Mgv\sin\theta$.
walkthrough: Energy transferred per unit time is power. For a constant force parallel to motion, $P = Fv$, with $v$ the speed along the force direction.
Power supplied to P by the string is $T v$, where $T$ is string tension. Because velocity is constant and resistive forces are negligible, resultant force is zero.
For hanging block Q moving down at speed $v$, $T = mg$. So power delivered via the string is $mgv$. This is statement 1.
For block P, kinetic energy is constant since $v$ is constant, so all energy to P becomes gravitational potential energy. In time $t$, distance up slope is $vt$ and vertical rise is $vt\sin\theta$.
Rate of gain of potential energy is $Mg \times$ vertical speed $= Mg(v\sin\theta) = Mgv\sin\theta$. This is statement 2, and constant velocity requires $mgv = Mgv\sin\theta$.
Statement 3, $(M+m)gv$, is the sum of two different rates and has no physical meaning for P alone. Only 1 and 2 are valid. This is option A.
